title: Embedded systems
specPoints: 1.1.3 The purpose and characteristics of **embedded systems**; examples of embedded systems
Compare embedded with general-purpose computers; justify why a device uses an embedded system
learn: Define an embedded system and give at least five everyday examples
List the characteristics: dedicated function, built into a larger device, limited resources, software in ROM/firmware, often real-time, low power and cost
Explain why a device uses an embedded system rather than a general-purpose computer
Identify embedded and non-embedded computers from descriptions
Link embedded systems to low-level languages (2.5) and to the micro:bit/ESP32 boards used in club
hook: Count the computers in your kitchen. Not the laptop — the washing machine, the microwave, the dishwasher, the boiler, the smart meter, the toaster with a timer. Each has a processor running one program it will run for its whole life. There are far more of those than there are laptops in the world.

video.title: The computers you don't see
video.brief: 3 minutes. A kitchen, then a car, then a hospital ward, with embedded processors highlighted one by one. Then a split: a laptop (runs anything, keyboard and screen, OS, GBs of RAM) versus a washing-machine controller (one job, buttons and a dial, firmware in ROM, KBs of RAM). Characteristics appear as labels. End with the question 'why not just put a PC in the washing machine?' and the answers: cost, size, power, reliability, start-up time.

p: An **embedded system** is a computer system built into a larger device to perform a **dedicated function**. It has a processor, memory and input/output like any computer, but it runs **one fixed program** (often called **firmware**, stored in ROM or flash) and the user usually doesn't think of it as a computer at all. Examples: washing machine controller, microwave, digital watch, car engine management unit, traffic lights, pacemaker, printer, smart thermostat, the controller inside a hard drive.

list: **Dedicated** — designed for one task or a small set of tasks; the program rarely or never changes.
**Built in** — part of a larger mechanical or electrical device; often no keyboard/screen, just buttons, sensors and small displays.
**Limited resources** — a small, cheap processor and little memory, enough for the job and no more.
**Firmware in ROM** — software stored permanently; starts instantly; cannot easily be altered by the user.
**Real-time** — many must respond within a guaranteed time (airbag, ABS brakes, pacemaker).
**Low power and cost** — runs for years on a battery or mains with minimal heat; manufactured cheaply in volume.
**Reliable** — fewer components and no general OS means fewer things to go wrong; often runs for years without a restart.

explain.code:
Embedded system                                  General-purpose computer (laptop, phone)
One program, fixed function                      Runs many programs; user installs more
Firmware in ROM; instant start                   Operating system loaded from storage; boots
Small, cheap processor; KB–MB of memory          Powerful processor; GB of memory
Low power; small; little or no cooling           Higher power; fans; larger
Simple interface: buttons, sensors, LEDs         Keyboard, touchscreen, full display
Very reliable; rarely updated                    Updated often; more can go wrong
after: Exam logic for 'why use an embedded system in X': pick the characteristics that matter for X. A pacemaker: reliability, low power, real-time response, small size. A washing machine: low cost, one function, simple controls, no need to run other software.

p: A device is embedded if the computer is *inside* something else and does *one job*. A smart TV is a borderline case the exam avoids; a games console and a smartphone are general-purpose (they run many apps). If a question says 'identify which of these are embedded systems', apply the two tests: inside a larger device? dedicated function?

Embedded systems are why low-level languages still matter (2.5.1: tight memory and timing); their programs are often written in C or assembly and compiled, never interpreted. The micro:bit and ESP32 boards you may have used in club are tiny general-purpose boards used to *build* embedded systems.

simple.h: A computer inside something else, doing one job
p: Washing machine, microwave, car engine controller, traffic lights, pacemaker. Each has a small processor running one program forever.

list: Hidden inside the device; buttons and sensors instead of keyboard and screen.
Low power; very reliable; often must react within a set time.

p: Too expensive, too big, too much power, takes time to start, and can crash. The washing machine needs none of a laptop's abilities.

keyterms.def: A computer system with a dedicated function built into a larger device.
Designed to carry out one specific task or a small fixed set of tasks.
Software stored permanently in ROM/flash that controls a device.
A system that must respond to inputs within a guaranteed time.
A computer that can run many different programs for many purposes.

try.title: 1. Embedded or not?
p: Classify and give the reason using the two tests: microwave · laptop · car ABS controller · smartphone · digital thermometer · games console · pacemaker · smart doorbell · desktop PC · lift control panel · e-reader · robot vacuum cleaner.

try.title: 2. Match characteristic to device
p: For each device choose the **two** most important embedded characteristics and explain why: pacemaker · traffic lights · washing machine · car airbag controller · smart meter.

try.title: 3. Design brief
p: You are designing the controller for a greenhouse vent that opens when it is too hot. List: inputs (sensors), outputs, the one program it runs (as 5–6 lines of pseudocode), where the program is stored, roughly how much memory it needs, and why a Raspberry Pi running Linux would be a poor choice compared with a microcontroller.

try.title: 4. Simulate the firmware
p: This is the greenhouse controller as a loop: read a (fake) temperature, decide, act. Run it; then add hysteresis so the vent doesn't flap open and shut around 25°C (open at 26, close at 24).

try.title: 5. Real embedded boards
instructions: Look at one micro:bit project. Identify its inputs, outputs, dedicated function and where its program lives. Write it up as an embedded-system case study in four lines.

exam.q: Define the term **embedded system** and give **two** examples.
model: A computer system built into a larger device with a dedicated function / limited set of functions (1). Examples (any two): washing machine, microwave, car engine control unit, traffic lights, pacemaker, printer (1 each).
exam.commentary: Definition must have both ideas: inside a device, dedicated. Examples must be devices, not 'computers in cars' vaguely — name the controller or the appliance.

exam.q: A company manufactures smart central-heating thermostats. Explain **two** reasons why an embedded system is used rather than a general-purpose computer.
model: It only needs to perform one task (reading temperature and switching the boiler) (1), so a small, cheap processor and memory are sufficient, keeping the cost of each unit low (1). It must run reliably for years with low power / without crashing or updating (1), which a dedicated firmware system on a small device achieves better than a full OS on a general-purpose computer (1).
exam.commentary: Point + reason, both tied to the thermostat. Cost, size, power, reliability and instant start are all acceptable angles.

model: Any two: dedicated to one function; built into a larger device; limited processing power/memory; software stored in ROM as firmware; low power consumption; often real-time (1 each).
exam.commentary: Characteristics of the *system*, not examples of devices.

home: List ten embedded systems you interacted with today, in order. For three of them write the inputs, outputs and dedicated function. For one, explain why it is not a general-purpose computer in two sentences.
